verses.verse:
अष्ट छिद्रासु बंशीषु गान्धारद्वय कल्पना।
नव छिद्रासु बंशीषु पंचमौ द्विस्थितौ मतौ।४३।
verses.text: In eight-holed bānsurīs the two Gāndhāras are provided; in nine-holed bānsurīs Pa is held to stand in two places.

commentary.text: That is, in the eight-hole bānsurī, along with Niṣāda, both Gāndhāras are also provided. And in the nine-hole bānsurī there is provision for playing Pañcama from two places: one comes out with all the holes open, and the other with all the holes closed. This too is a marvel of this instrument which is not found in other instruments.

Of these two holes, from one only the Pa of the middle saptaka (octave) comes out, and from the other the Pa of all three octaves. The smallest āḍī bansī (transverse bānsurī) I have is of aluminium pipe. If a small piece of that pipe were cut off, kept as a ring, and opened out flat, its length would be about one inch and one sūt (a small unit of length); this we can call the paridhimāna (measure of the inner circumference). The full length is seven inches and four sūt. Measured from the mukharandhra (mouth-hole) it is six inches four sūt. Its first hole is eight and a half sūt above the open (mukta) Pañcama at the bottom; this is taken as Dhaivata. The distance from Dhaivata to Niṣāda is 7 sūt. The distance from Niṣāda to Ṣaḍja, that is the third hole, is 4 sūt. The distance of Ṛṣabha, that is the fourth hole, from Ṣaḍja is six and a half sūt. Then Gāndhāra is five and a half from there, and the distance of tīvra Madhyama is 5 sūt. Thus the total distance from the open part at the bottom up to tīvra Madhyama at the top comes to thirty-six and a half sūt. In this bānsurī, besides the six holes, there is a seventh hole too, for the Pañcama of the middle octave. Its distance from the tīvra Madhyama hole above is two and a half sūt, but this hole lies on the side opposite to the other holes, and it is easily closed with the thumb. Since this bānsurī is not even seven times as long as its inner paridhimāna, the distances of its holes differ somewhat from the calculation given earlier. The hole distances given in the book are taken from the centre point. In this bānsurī a separate hole for the komal notes would have been impractical, so players draw out 12 notes from only six [holes] by their skill. If the human finger were two sūt thinner, it could have had more holes. The Ṣaḍja that sounds in this bānsurī when the top three holes are closed matches the upper (tār) octave of the harmonium's second black key. If the harmonium differs somewhat, the bānsurī can be altered in the same proportion. Now the measurements of the larger bānsurī, made for kālī 1 (the first black key), are written next.

The total length of this bānsurī is 8 inches. Measured from the outside, the paridhi (circumference) is 15 sūt in all, that is one and a half inches. The inner circumference, that is the girth, is a little more than 11 sūt. The length from Pañcama to the mukharandhra (mouth-hole) is 6 inches 8 sūt. That is, from the mouth-hole down to the open (mukta) Pañcama this bānsurī is six times its inner paridhimāna (measure of the inner circumference). It has 7 holes in all, of which one hole is at the back and six holes are on the front. The distance from the open Pañcama, that is the very end of the bānsurī, to the first hole, that is Dhaivata, is nine sūt in all. The distance from the first hole to the second is less than seven sūt. The third hole is four sūt from there. The distance from the third to the fourth hole is six sūt. The distance from the fourth to the fifth hole is also six sūt. The distance from the fifth to the sixth hole is five and a half sūt. And the seventh, the hole made at the back, is at a distance of four sūt. Thus the total distance from mandra Pañcama to madhya Pañcama is about 9+6+6+5+4+4 sūt. From there the distance to the mouth-hole is 26 sūt.

If a bānsurī is made on the basis of the measurements written above, eighty per cent of the bānsurī will come out in tune. Yet it can be a hundred per cent right only when, matching those holes to the pitch of the harmonium, the golāī (roundness) of some holes is made smaller or larger by means of the pitch. A bānsurī made on the basis of gaṇita (calculation) alone may also be incomplete, because working out the calculation for the roundness of a hole and making it on the basis of that calculation are both needlessly very difficult tasks. So, like salt in dāl, many tasks rest on estimate. So svara and Īśvara cannot be attained on the basis of calculation and logic. This is the meaning of the śloka written below.
